newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission proposes wider worker consultation laws.
newsitem.headline: Commission proposes wider worker consultation laws.

text.p: European Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn called on Wednesday for EU rules to would oblige companies to set up national systems for consulting their workers on decisions that affect their jobs.
The rules should contain sanctions on firms that failed to consult their employees properly and in good time, Flynn told a news conference.
He was expanding on a European Commission paper which asks trade union and company representatives to consider the need for European Union rules on consulting workers at national level.
"We need to look at a better way of (enforcing) information and consultation...notably by nullifying decisions made in violation of the relevant rules," Flynn said.

The 15-member EU already has general rules obliging large multinationals to consult workers, and patchier rules requiring national firms to consult employees on a number of specific issues, such as imminent collective redundancies.
But the rules were "not perfect (and) not complete", Flynn said, and Ireland and Britain had no national consultation laws.
Common rules would eliminate distortions of competition and ensure equal treatment for workers throughout the EU, the Commission's consultation paper argues.

New EU rules were also needed because some firms did not consult their workers widely or early enough, Fylnn said, adding that he hoped EU governments would now lift their opposition to tougher sanctions on firms breaching the rules.
The Commission's initiative comes in the wake of a much-criticised decision by car maker Renault to close its Belgian plant at Vilvoorde, with the loss of 3,100 jobs.
Renault would have been forced to reverse its decision if member states had accepted a 1991 Commission proposal which included tough sanctions, Flynn said.

He said he hoped the European employers' group UNICE, which has in the past rejected the idea of general EU rules, would now accept that consulting workers was good for business because it helped get the best out of employees and boost productivity.
